name: @fossil-lang/corpus
description: The executable half of the corpus contract: the guards that make a convention checkable, and the conformance corpus that makes two readers agree. The prose half is /docs/format on the documentation site. Never published; the pnpm-workspace entry is for resolution, not for npm.
//no-build: There is no build here and no dependency to install. This was a Next.js site until the documentation was centralised — twelve pages with their own bundler, their own search index and nine runtime dependencies identical, version for version, to the ones next door. The pages are `apps/docs/content/docs/format/`; what stayed is the part that executes.
//guards: `guards/` has no npm dependencies and no build step. It needs `node` and the `duckdb` binary, so `pnpm check`, `pnpm self-test` and `pnpm fixture` run in a checkout where nothing has been installed — which is the position the third party this format is for is in.
//conformance: `conformance/` is the other half: the guards check that a corpus IS what the conventions say, and the conformance corpus checks that independent readers ADDRESS it the same way. THREE do, and none of them wrote `expected.json`: the plain-Node `conformance/reader.mjs`, the published TypeScript `resolveCorpus` (`packages/graph/tests/conformance.test.ts`, a **pnpm** test in another package — moving an address here turns it red and `node guards/self-test.mjs` will not tell you), and `fossil_graph::address`, which runs natively in `crates/fossil-graph/tests/conformance.rs` and as wasm32 through `conformance/wasm-reader.mjs`. It was two, and both were JavaScript.
//containers: `conformance/containers.mjs` is the third question, and it is the one a change of container has to pass BEFORE a writer emits one: the same graph written both ways answers identically. `packages/graph/tests/containers.test.ts` asks it of the published module. Two readers moved and diffed in advance is the whole rule — after the writer moves, the only corpus that exists is the new one and there is nothing left to compare against. It runs BEFORE `check.mjs conformance/corpus`, which is 17/17: this said `knowingly 16/17` because the checked-in corpus shipped `by_source.parquet` beside `by_source/`, and it has not since the writer moved to one container and `fossil-mcp` stopped registering its views over that file. A step behind a red one never runs, which is why the ordering is worth stating and the number is worth measuring rather than remembering.
//wasm-leg: `pnpm test` here passes `--without-wasm`, and that is not a weakening. This directory's claim is that it runs on `node` plus a `duckdb` binary in a checkout where nothing has been installed; the wasm reader needs `packages/graph/pkg/`, a Rust toolchain and `wasm-bindgen-cli`. So the refusal is explicit and the default is not: `pnpm conformance` runs every leg and FAILS if the build output is absent, which is what `.github/workflows/pnpm-ci.yml` runs after it has built one. A leg that skipped itself when its dependency was missing is how a conformance suite comes to pass over nothing.
//test: `pnpm test` is the guards' own self-test: a conforming corpus is written in both containers, every guard passes on it, and then every guard is required to FIRE against a corpus broken in exactly one way. There is deliberately no guard over the prose that describes this — one existed, it checked that a cited line existed rather than that it said what the page claimed, and 159 dead references accumulated under it with CI green throughout. A guard that measures the artifact is worth writing; a guard that measures a page's punctuation buys the appearance of one.

scripts.test: node guards/self-test.mjs && node conformance/containers.mjs && node guards/check.mjs conformance/corpus && node conformance/verify.mjs --without-wasm
